messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Marco

Marco was twenty-three when he was taken off a street corner in Monterrey by men in an unmarked sedan. He had been waiting for a cousin who never came. The car was white with tinted windows and a dent in the rear panel—details he would never forget. They drove him to a warehouse on the outskirts of the city, where he was held for four days. The men who took him wore no uniforms, but they carried themselves with the casual authority of people accustomed to inflicting pain without consequence. They asked him questions about his brother's involvement in local politics, questions Marco could not answer because he did not know the answer. They used electricity, water, and their fists. On the third day, one of them laughed while Marco was crying. That laugh—the incongruity of it, the pleasure taken in his suffering—lodged itself somewhere deep in his nervous system. When he was finally released, dumped on a rural road with instructions never to speak of what happened, Marco made his way north. He was twenty-four by the time he crossed into Texas with forged papers and a name that was not entirely his own.

Now, at twenty-six and living in Houston, Marco works as a maid in a downtown hotel. The job is steady, the pay is modest, and it requires him to be invisible—which he prefers. But invisibility is impossible to maintain when your body has learned to read threat in every shadow. Two years have passed since the warehouse, and Marco has come to understand his own mind as a place where safety is always provisional, always conditional on his vigilance.

Certain cars stop him cold. He was in the parking garage last month, carrying linens to the third floor, when a white sedan pulled in two spaces away. His hands began to shake. He dropped an entire cart of towels and had to tell his supervisor he was unwell. The car was a Camry, not a sedan, and the dent was in the wrong place, but his body did not care about these distinctions. He had come to expect that similarity itself was threat—that the universe was full of near-misses that might, at any moment, become exact ones.

He does not watch the news. A coworker had been watching something on her phone about a police raid, and Marco left the break room and did not return until she was gone. He avoids the hotel's security office, takes the long route past the front desk when he can, and feels his stomach tighten whenever he sees a man in a uniform—even the bellhops, even the parking attendants. When his ex-wife's new partner, a police officer, came to pick up their daughter for a weekend visit, Marco stayed in his apartment. He had not seen his daughter in three months. The guilt of that absence was enormous, but the fear of being near a uniformed man was larger.

What troubles Marco most, though, is something he cannot quite name. Last week, his sister called with good news—she had been accepted to nursing school. In the moment before Marco could stop himself, he felt something light in his chest, something almost like joy. The feeling terrified him. Joy felt like a luxury he had forfeited in that warehouse, like a betrayal of the person he had been before, like tempting fate. He smoked three cigarettes in rapid succession and told his sister he would call her back. He has been smoking more—a pack a day now, sometimes more when he is alone.

He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, his heart already racing before his eyes open. He lies still, listening for sounds in the hallway, checking the locks on his door even though he has already checked them. When his neighbor knocked on his door last Tuesday to ask about a package delivery, Marco flinched so violently that the man stepped back, alarmed. The touch itself—even the possibility of touch—sends electricity through him.

He came to the clinic because his sister insisted, because she said she was worried he was disappearing, because she said that the brother she knew would not let fear make him a ghost. Marco is not sure what he is hoping for, only that the constant vigilance is exhausting, that he cannot keep running from cars and uniforms and the inexplicable terror of his own safety, and that he is terrified that if he stops running, if he stops checking the locks and waking in the night, then the thing he fears most will finally arrive.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: Patient is 26, but vignette states Marco was 23 at time of trauma and is now 26, which is mathematically consistent with the vignette's timeline (trauma occurred ~2 years ago). However, the vignette explicitly states 'Marco was twenty-three' at the time of abduction and 'now, at twenty-six' - this is internally consistent but the stated age of 26 should be verified as current age.: Age representation is present and consistent with patient data (current age 26, trauma occurred when patient was 23-24).

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
